pass_a_gloss: Logos 1. [Lemma, Isaiah 1:1:] Vision which Isaiah son of Amoz saw, which he saw against Judaea and against Jerusalem in the reign of Uzziah and Jotham and Ahaz and Hezekiah, who reigned over Judaea. Someone would not, I think, lie saying that about the holy prophets, that they received not only the knowledge of the things to be, the Holy Spirit making the thing shine bright to them, and sounding it into mind, but indeed that at times they became beholders of the things themselves. The blessed prophet Isaiah then seems to have beheld with the eyes of the mind the sufferings that will be in times against Judaea, on the one hand the ranks of the enemies ravaging the land, on the other the cities made desert, and houses being burned, and as many things as are done by enemies by the laws of war; for this reason it has been written at the front of the prophecy: Vision which Isaiah son of Amoz saw, against Judaea and against Jerusalem. And he usefully marks the times of the kings, so that God may appear speaking the things in the prophet suitably to the ways of each. [Lemma, Isaiah 1:2-3:] Hear, heaven, and give ear, earth, because the Lord spoke: Sons I begot and lifted up, but they set me aside. The ox knew the one who acquired it, and the donkey the manger of its lord; but Israel did not know me, and the people did not understand me. What the thing is, what the account, and what it would wish to show, it is necessary to look around at. For the blessed prophet as it were calls to witness both heaven and earth, and doing this not without God, but he says the words are not his own, but rather God's; signifying through this that in every way and wholly they will come out to an end, and terrifying the hearers with the fears of suffering. For it is impossible for God to speak falsely; and at the same time also arranging that, as I think. For since he was about to make the foretellings against Judaea and Jerusalem, and to announce beforehand sufferings beyond every word, and the incurable misfortunes, he was not ignorant that in every way and wholly those to whom the word [was] would be sharpened toward angers. He says then that the Lord spoke such things to them, pushing aside most skilfully the rage of the unholy, and as it were shaming away the unjust angers. For if he was taken on as a mediator and minister, and should be ferrying across the words from above and from God, how would someone justly be angry at him? Rather, how [would] not against God who had spoken the things from ange[r] [the section breaks off].
pass_b_english: Logos 1. “The vision which Isaiah son of Amoz saw, which he saw against Judah and against Jerusalem in the reign of Uzziah and Jotham and Ahaz and Hezekiah, who reigned over Judah” (Isaiah 1:1).

I do not think anyone would be speaking falsely if he said this about the holy prophets: they received not only the knowledge of things to come, as the Holy Spirit made the matter shine clear to them and sounded it into their minds, but at times they also became eyewitnesses of the events themselves. So the blessed prophet Isaiah seems to have seen with the eyes of the mind the sufferings that would come upon Judah in due time: here the ranks of the enemy ravaging the land, there the cities laid waste, houses set on fire, and all that enemies do by the laws of war. That is why this stands written at the head of the prophecy: “The vision which Isaiah son of Amoz saw against Judah and against Jerusalem” (Isaiah 1:1).
He usefully marks the times of the kings, so that God may be seen to speak through the prophet what suited the ways of each.

“Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: Sons I have begotten and raised up, but they have rejected Me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger; but Israel does not know Me, and My people have not understood Me” (Isaiah 1:2–3).

What the matter is, what the reasoning is, and what it means to show, we must look into closely. The blessed prophet solemnly calls, as it were, both heaven and earth to witness, and in doing so he does not act without God; rather, he says that the words are not his own but God's. By this he signifies that they will come to pass in every way and without fail, and he dismays his hearers with dread of suffering, for it is impossible for God to speak falsely.

At the same time, as I think, he is also securing something else. He was about to make his predictions against Judah and Jerusalem, and to announce beforehand sufferings beyond all words and incurable calamities, and he knew well that those to whom the message was addressed would in every way be sharpened to anger. So he says that the Lord spoke these things to them, and so most skilfully turns aside the fury of the ungodly and, as it were, shames their unjust anger into silence. For if he was taken on as a mediator and servant, and was carrying across words from above and from God, how could anyone justly be angry with him? Or rather, how would whatever they did in anger not be aimed against God who had spoken…

choices.english: I do not think anyone would be speaking falsely
choices.why: The potential optative: one would not lie to say that the prophets also saw events; it is not that no one dared lie.
rejected: No one would dare to lie

choices.why: The prophets at times saw the events, not only knew them.
